scenario: Today's generative track fills in what generative recommendation misses when it simply continues a user's history with more SIDs. ReSID finds that long-tail items are mostly pruned by beam search early in decoding, so it keeps tail prefixes alive while decoding. TriGen handles the feed a user enters after clicking an item, letting each request decide how much the click overrides history. TraGR predicts several future steps at once and passes along the candidates it did not choose, weighted by probability. SimRec takes another direction, training the whole search, ask, and recommend loop of a recommendation agent with a simulated user and reinforcement learning, so it learns to check candidates and recover after a rejection.

papers.title: ReSID: Rethinking Long-Tail Retrieval in Generative Recommendation through Item Reachability
papers.authors: Muyu Zou, Shunye Tang, Yi Xu, Haibo Xing, Yandong Wang, Lingyu Mu, Jinxin Hu
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) represents items with discrete Semantic IDs (SIDs) and casts retrieval as sequence generation. Under skewed interaction distributions and tight serving budgets, GR struggles to retrieve long-tail items. In this work, we are the first to study long-tail reachability across the complete pipeline of SID construction, decoding, and matching. We find that under equal code lengths, parallel SID construction consistently outperforms sequential SIDs on tail items. Moreover, even when full generation fails, decoded sequences carry locally consistent information that retrieves relevant tail items via partial matching. Yet this recovery is bounded by upstream search, failing once beam search prunes all prefixes completable within a fixed mismatch tolerance. Motivated by these findings, we propose ReSID to jointly preserve and recover tail candidates. Built on long parallel SIDs, ReSID pairs popularity-debiased and user-semantic-aware beam search to keep promising paths alive with partial SID matching to recover items from surviving tokens. ReSID achieves state-of-the-art long-tail retrieval while maintaining competitive overall accuracy, with lower latency and higher throughput under narrow beams. ReSID is deployed in our production system, serving main user traffic with substantial business gains. We release our complete code and model checkpoints to support full reproducibility and real-world deployment at https://github.com/Gabriel-reina/ReSID.
papers.note: 生产部署、公开代码及检查点；长尾召回可迁移到UGC候选召回
papers.summary: Generative recommendation encodes each item as a string of Semantic ID tokens and generates them one position at a time with beam search, and cold long-tail items are hard to retrieve this way. The authors take apart the whole chain from encoding through decoding to matching and find that tail items are mostly lost early in decoding: on Amazon Industrial, 62.5% of tail targets have already fallen out of the beam after just two tokens. They also find that parallel SIDs, which split the vector into segments and quantize each separately, treat the tail better than sequential SIDs that quantize residuals layer by layer. The reason is that an error at one position does not spill into later ones, so a partly wrong sequence still keeps useful positions. ReSID therefore damps popularity bias and adds a user-semantic score inside beam search so tail prefixes survive, then allows a match even when some positions disagree. It now serves main traffic, raising ad revenue by 1.3% and the long-tail exposure share by 4.0%. ==Tail items are often pruned during decoding, and looser matching afterwards cannot bring them back==.

papers.title: TriGen: A Generative Paradigm for Trigger-Induced Recommendation
papers.authors: Muyu Zou, Haibo Xing, Shunye Tang, Liyan Tie, Lingyu Mu, Yandong Wang, Jinxin Hu
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation typically operates under the User-Induced Recommendation (UIR) setting, predicting target items by autoregressively generating semantic IDs as a passive continuation of long-term user history. However, this paradigm overlooks Trigger-Induced Recommendation (TIR), an essential industrial scenario where a user click triggers an immediate follow-up feed. In TIR, recommendations must dynamically align with the instant trigger intent without compromising historical preference continuity. Traditional TIR methods rely on discriminative scoring and cannot guide token-level generation, while existing generative models lack mechanisms to reconcile this structural tension. To address this challenge, we propose TriGen, establishing a tailored generative paradigm for trigger-induced recommendation. TriGen introduces calibrated tail injection to re-encode local history, adaptively arbitrates between persistent tastes and immediate impulses via dynamic gating, and applies position-specific transformations to sustain level-aware trigger guidance across decoding steps. Extensive offline evaluations confirm consistent gains over competitive baselines. Furthermore, online A/B tests across six country markets demonstrate significant revenue and GMV improvements, leading to the full production deployment of TriGen.
papers.note: 六个国家市场线上实验并已部署；触发意图与历史兴趣联合建模
papers.summary: E-commerce has a common kind of recommendation: a user clicks an item in the main feed and lands at once in a feed built around that item. The recommendations must follow the intent of that click without throwing away the user's long-term taste. Generative recommendation by default just continues the user's history with more SIDs, so one click is easily diluted in a long history, while traditional methods rely on discriminative scoring and cannot steer token-by-token generation. Alibaba International's TriGen appends several copies of the clicked item to the end of the history so it mainly reshapes recent behavior. It then uses a gate to decide per request whether to follow the click or the history more, and keeps injecting the click signal at every decoding position. In online experiments in six Southeast Asian countries, revenue rose 3.27% and GMV 0.90%, and it is now fully deployed. ==In click-triggered feeds, the hard part is how much the click should override history, and that changes every time==.

papers.title: SimRec: Learning to Search, Ask, and Recommend from Simulated Interaction
papers.authors: Yaxin Zhang, Xingyu Wu, Yuchen Yan, Yuqin Dai, Hong Zhao, Lixing Shen, Zhan Chen, Jian Shao, Yongliang Shen
papers.abstract: LLM-based recommendation agents can search catalogs, inspect products, ask users, and revise rejected recommendations. However, these behaviors are often governed by hand-designed workflows, while existing training methods optimize isolated components such as query rewriting or list ranking rather than the interaction policy as a whole. We present SimRec, a reinforcement learning framework that trains the full interaction policy of a tool-integrated recommendation agent. SimRec introduces two components. A task-anchored user simulator provides feedback on every recommendation: conditioned on the current task need rather than on user profile, and it can be an external LLM or the recommender itself under self-play. A task-aligned reward optimizes the whole trajectory with GRPO, crediting natural retrieval quality and valid tool use alongside the final hit, with training-only target injection to handle sparse hits over large catalogs. On ESCI and Amazon C4, SimRec improves the NDCG@100 of a Qwen3-4B agent from 32.23% to 35.42% and from 22.94% to 24.72%}, outperforming training-free agents on far larger backbones and task-aligned baselines on NDCG. Analysis shows that the trained agent verifies candidates, uses preferences, and recovers from rejected recommendations far more often than its untrained counterpart. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/SimRec .
papers.note: ESCI与Amazon C4离线提升；公开代码，交互策略联合训练
papers.summary: LLM-based recommendation agents can search a catalog, open product details, ask the user, and try another item after a rejection, but when to search, ask, or recommend is mostly a hand-written workflow. Existing training only practices single steps such as rewriting a query or ranking a list, so the outcome of the whole conversation never reaches the policy making those decisions. The authors find that such agents seldom check the candidates they retrieve, seldom consult the user's history, and rarely recover after a rejection, and a bigger model does not make up for it. SimRec trains the whole interaction with reinforcement learning: a simulated user who knows the task need but not the target item gives feedback on every recommendation, and the reward counts retrieval quality, valid tool use, and the final hit. On ESCI it lifts the NDCG@100 of a Qwen3-4B agent from 32.23% to 35.42%, beating untrained agents on much larger backbones. ==What recommendation agents lack is checking candidates and recovering after a rejection, and a bigger model does not supply it==.

papers.title: From Tokens to Behaviors: Rethinking Generative Recommendation for User Trajectory Prediction
papers.authors: Jiaqi Wang, Hanchen Yang, Hengyu Zhang, Hongxu Ma, Wenqi Rao, Hongyang Wang, Zhongbo Sun, Renliang Qian, Weixin Chen, Wengen Li, Jihong Guan, Shuigeng Zhou, Qingpeng Cai, Peng Jiang, Hong Cheng
papers.abstract: User behavior trajectory prediction (UBTP) aims to capture how a user's needs evolve over time by predicting the sequence of future interactions from that user's interaction history. Recent generative recommendation (GR) methods address this task through autoregressive generation of semantic IDs (SIDs). However, serial SID decoding couples token generation with behavior state transitions and requires multiple dependent steps per interaction. Discrete item feedback overlooks predictive uncertainty, and teacher-forced training leaves a training-inference gap in trajectory generation. To address these limitations, we propose TraGR, a behavior-aware generative recommendation framework that aligns generation, feedback, and learning with successive user behaviors. Its behavior-level architecture predicts SID tokens in parallel within each interaction and models behavioral transitions through recurrent state updates, with joint SID and item-level supervision. Probability feedback combines the selected behavior with a probability-weighted summary of alternatives to guide subsequent predictions. Relation-aware trajectory learning incorporates collaborative transition signals and later credit assignment into training on model-generated trajectories. Experiments on four public datasets demonstrate that TraGR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across different prediction horizons. Code: https://github.com/CalmaQi/GR4UBT.
papers.note: 四个公开数据集；行为轨迹生成，缺少线上验证
papers.summary: Most recommenders guess only the user's next click, while user trajectory prediction guesses the next several steps at once, such as buying running shoes and then sports socks and a water bottle. Generative recommendation does this by generating each item's SID token by token before moving to the next item, so the encoding within an item and the transitions between items are tangled in one chain. Worse, each step passes on only the chosen item: if the model gives socks 50% and running shoes 35%, later steps see only the socks and the shoe clue is lost. TraGR generates all SID positions of an item in parallel, moves between items with a recurrent state, passes on the chosen item plus a probability-weighted summary of the other candidates, and trains on trajectories the model generates itself. On four public datasets it beats the strongest baselines, and its lead holds at longer horizons. ==In trajectory prediction, candidates not chosen at one step are useful clues for the steps after it==.

deep_reading.title: From Tokens to Behaviors: Rethinking Generative Recommendation for User Trajectory Prediction
